name: Helsby hill fort
text: Your train passes near Helsby hill fort, on the train's {side}, an Iron Age fort on Helsby Hill, guarded by steep cliffs on two sides and by double earth banks on the others. The hill rises to 141 metres above the Cheshire Plain, with views over the Mersey estuary into Wales, and much of it belongs to the National Trust.

name: St Plegmund's Well
text: Your train passes near St Plegmund's Well, on the train's {side}, a stone-lined holy well named after Plegmund, who is believed to have lived as a hermit nearby before he became Archbishop of Canterbury. It is first mentioned in a document of 1301, and it is said to have been used for baptisms into the 20th century.

name: St Peter's Church, Plemstall
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church, Plemstall, on the train's {side}, standing alone at the end of a country lane. It is believed to be on the spot where Plegmund, later Archbishop of Canterbury, lived as a hermit in the ninth century, on raised ground in the old marshes once called the Isle of Chester, and most of the present building is 15th-century.

name: Black Lake
text: Your train passes near Black Lake, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve in Delamere Forest where a floating raft of sphagnum moss covers about half the water. It is a quaking bog, in a hollow left by a block of ice that melted at the end of the last Ice Age, and it is known for its uncommon dragonflies.

name: Oakmere Hall
text: Your train passes near Oakmere Hall, on the train's {side}, a house of 1867 that was one of the largest designed by the Chester architect John Douglas. It was built for two Runcorn merchants who went bankrupt after losing all their ships in the blockade of Charleston; from 1943 it was a rehabilitation centre for injured miners, and it is now flats.

name: Hartford Manor
text: Your train passes near Hartford Manor, on the train's {side}, a former country house said to have been given a new stone front in about 1820 for John Marshall. Thomas Marshall, a wealthy salt merchant from Northwich, had bought the estate in 1774, and the house was then called Hartford Green Bank Manor.

name: St John the Baptist's Church, Hartford
text: Your train passes near St John the Baptist's Church, Hartford, on the train's {side}, built in the 1870s to designs by John Douglas when the first church of 1824 had grown too small. Its tower followed in 1887, and a ring of six bells was dedicated ten years later.

name: Dutton Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Dutton Viaduct, over the River Weaver and the Weaver Navigation. Finished in December 1836, it was the longest viaduct on the Grand Junction Railway, about 460 metres long and 18 metres high, and it has carried trains ever since 1837.

name: Rocksavage
text: Your train passes near Rocksavage, on the train's {side}, the ruins of an Elizabethan mansion built in the 1560s for Sir John Savage. It was one of the great houses of Cheshire, and James I visited it in 1617, but it was abandoned in the early 18th century and only ruins were left by 1782.

name: Castle Park House
text: Your train passes near Castle Park House, on the train's {side}, a late 18th-century house said to stand on the site of Frodsham Castle, which burnt down in 1654. It was extended in the 1850s, when Edward Kemp laid out its gardens, and the house and most of its park are now held by a charitable trust.

name: Norton Water Tower
text: Your train passes near Norton Water Tower, on the train's {side}, a round red sandstone tower topped by an iron tank that holds 650,000 gallons. Built between 1888 and 1892, it stands on the pipeline that brings water from Lake Vyrnwy in North Wales to Liverpool, and a Latin inscription around it says where the water comes from.

name: Daresbury Laboratory
text: Your train passes near Daresbury Laboratory, on the train's {side}, a national science laboratory opened by the Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, in 1967. It began as a nuclear physics laboratory, and it now carries out research in accelerator science, medicine, physics, chemistry, engineering and computing.

name: Vulcan Foundry
text: Your train passes near the Vulcan Foundry, on the train's {side}, which built locomotives for railways around the world from 1832 to 1970. It was set up after the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, and Robert Stephenson was a partner for a few years.

name: Sankey Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the Sankey Viaduct, known locally as the Nine Arches, built by George Stephenson between 1828 and 1830 to carry the Liverpool and Manchester Railway over Sankey Brook and the Sankey Canal. It was made high enough for the masts of the canal's sailing barges, and it has been called the earliest major railway viaduct in the world.

name: St Nicholas Church, Sutton
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church, Sutton, on the train's {side}, built in 1847 to 1849 to designs by Sharpe and Paley of Lancaster. King's College, Cambridge, its patron, gave £1,270 towards it to mark four hundred years since the college was founded, and the tower was added in 1897.

name: Rainhill
text: Your train passes near Rainhill, on the train's {side}, the village where the Rainhill Trials were held in 1829 to choose a locomotive for the new Liverpool and Manchester Railway. Stephenson's Rocket won, and in 1979 a cavalcade of trains, with replicas of the winner and the runner-up, marked 150 years since the trials.

name: Rainhill station
text: Rainhill station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1830 with the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, and it is one of the oldest passenger stations in the world. At its western end is George Stephenson's skew bridge, which carries the main road over the line and was the first bridge ever to cross a railway at an angle.

name: Stadt Moers Park
text: Your train passes near Stadt Moers Park, on the train's {side}, a country park between Whiston and Huyton on land once used for coal mining, a brickworks and a rubbish tip. Knowsley Council began turning it into a park in 1983, and named it after Knowsley's twin town, Moers in Germany.

name: 159, 161 and 163 Crow Lane East
text: Your train passes near 159, 161 and 163 Crow Lane East, on the train's {side}, a terrace of three thatched, cruck-framed cottages from the 16th century, among the oldest lived-in buildings in Newton-le-Willows. They are known locally for their elaborate Christmas displays and lights, put up for charity.

name: Westwood Power Station
text: Your train passes near the site of Westwood Power Station, on the train's {side}, a coal-fired power station beside the Leeds and Liverpool Canal whose first generating set started up in 1951. Its two cooling towers were demolished in January 1989, and the site is now a business park.

name: Old St Ann's Church, Warrington
text: Your train passes near the old St Ann's Church, Warrington, on the train's {side}, built in the 1860s to designs by John Douglas. It closed for worship in 1995 and has been an indoor climbing centre since 1996; from the 1960s to the 1980s it was heated by steam from the brewery next door.

name: Light Oaks Hall
text: Your train passes near Light Oaks Hall, on the train's {side}, an early 17th-century gentry house near Glazebury. Only two bays of a larger house survive, and a panel inside bears the date 1657.

name: Astley and Bedford Mosses
text: Your train passes near Astley and Bedford Mosses, on the train's {side}, among the last fragments of Chat Moss, the raised peat bog that once covered a wide area north of the River Mersey. The bog began to form after the last Ice Age, about 10,000 years ago, and Astley Moss has been a Site of Special Scientific Interest since 1989.

name: St Mary the Virgin's Church, Eccles
text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin's Church, Eccles, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church on a site used for worship since Norman times or earlier. In the Middle Ages it was the centre of a large parish that reached from Pendleton to part of Chat Moss, and for several hundred years it was the only church in it.

name: Warrington Transporter Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Warrington Transporter Bridge, on the train's {side}, a steel bridge over the River Mersey built in 1916 and 1917 to link the two halves of Joseph Crosfield and Sons' chemical and soap works. It first carried railway wagons, was converted for road vehicles in 1940, and fell out of use in about 1964.

name: Hefferston Grange
text: Your train passes near Hefferston Grange, on the train's {side}, a Georgian country house built in 1741 for Philip Henry Warburton. From 1921 it was part of a hospital for people with tuberculosis, and the National Health Service sold it in 1986.

name: Winsford Mine
text: Your train passes near Winsford Mine, on the train's {side}, Britain's oldest working mine, which digs rock salt used to grit the country's roads in winter. The salt was found by accident by workers looking for coal to heat salt pans, and the mine first opened in 1844.

name: Lea Hall
text: Your train passes near Lea Hall, on the train's {side}, an early 18th-century brick house built for the Lowndes family. Its large hipped roof has a viewing platform on top, and the initials J V over the door are for Joseph Verdin, who owned it in the 19th century.

name: Churche's Mansion
text: Your train passes near Churche's Mansion, on the train's {side}, a black-and-white timber-framed house of 1577, built for the merchant Richard Churche. It is one of the few buildings to survive the Great Fire of Nantwich in 1583, and in the early 1930s it was saved from being shipped to the United States.

name: St Mary's Church, Nantwich
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Nantwich, on the train's {side}, a 14th-century red sandstone church with an octagonal tower. It has been called the Cathedral of South Cheshire, and some think it one of the finest medieval churches in England.

name: Churton Memorial Fountain
text: Your train passes near the Churton Memorial Fountain, on the train's {side}, a drinking fountain that John Churton put up in 1882 in memory of his parents and his wife. Lions' heads spout water at the front and back, with troughs for animals at the sides, and it was moved along Brownlow Street in the early 1930s because it got in the way of traffic.

name: BAE Systems Radway Green
text: Your train passes near Radway Green, on the train's {side}, a factory set up as a Royal Ordnance Factory in 1940 to make ammunition. BAE Systems took it over in 1987, and it makes small arms ammunition for the British armed forces.

name: Hardings Wood Junction
text: Your train passes near Hardings Wood Junction, on the train's {side}, where the Macclesfield Canal joins the Trent and Mersey Canal. It opened in 1831, and just beyond it the Macclesfield Canal crosses over the Trent and Mersey on an aqueduct.

name: The Bleeding Wolf
text: Your train passes near the Bleeding Wolf, on the train's {side}, a pub at Scholar Green built in 1936 for Robinson's Brewery of Stockport. Its unusual name is said to come from a legend in which King John rewarded a local forester for saving him from a wolf.

name: Macclesfield Sunday School
text: Your train passes near the Old Sunday School in Macclesfield, on the train's {side}, built on Roe Street for a Sunday school that had begun in 1796 with 40 children. It had 1,127 boys and 1,324 girls on its books when it opened, and it is now part of Macclesfield Museums.

name: Arighi Bianchi
text: Your train passes near Arighi Bianchi, on the train's {side}, a furniture shop founded in 1854 by two Italians from near Lake Como. Its four-storey cast iron and glass front was inspired by the Crystal Palace, and it was saved from demolition in 1973 after a campaign that John Betjeman supported.

name: St Peter's Church, Prestbury
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church, Prestbury, on the train's {side}, probably the fourth church on the site. The third, a Norman chapel, still stands in the churchyard, and there is good evidence of a church here before the Norman Conquest: the village's name means priest's enclosure.

name: Adlington Hall
text: Your train passes near Adlington Hall, on the train's {side}, a country house whose Great Hall was built between 1480 and 1505. The Legh family has lived on the site since the early 14th century, and an organ was put into the Great Hall after Parliamentary forces had occupied the house in the Civil War.

name: Bramhall
text: Your train passes near Bramhall, on the train's {side}, a large village recorded in the Domesday Book as Bramale. The name comes from Old English words for broom, the shrub, and for a nook or secret place, probably by water.

name: John Millington
text: Your train passes near the John Millington, on the train's {side}, a pub in a late 17th-century house built for John Millington, a local alderman who died in 1694. The house was later used for hand-loom silk weaving, and it reopened as a pub in 2006 after Hydes Brewery restored it.
